identifying_description: Basic Construction: The garment hangs from and is supported by a long wooden crossbar along its top edge. The foundation layers of the costume consist of an inner and outer layer of fabric, which serve as the base to which the decorative lappets are attached. There is a net-like panel in the middle of the top half at the front of the costume, through which the dancer can look. The exterior of the costume is decorated with a series of overlapping fabric panels (“lappets”), of varying shapes, sizes, and decorations. Foundation Layers (Top Edge):Structural Element: long wooden board, wrapped in plain/indigo dyed roughly woven fabric. Along the bottom edge of the board is a long tubular element (roll of fabric, bound with caning (or another reed-like material) that has been sewn to the wooden board. This is visible through tears in the sides of the base fabric, and reinforces what was visible in the x-rays. These structural elements support the shape and weight of the entire costume and create depth, allowing space for the head padding.In the middle of the tubular roll of fabric is an additional square-shaped pillow, placed inline with the netted panel, this serves as a padded element for the wearer’s head. Base Fabric: various fabrics cover the wooden board + tubular element and act as the base to which the exterior decorations (e.g. lappets) are attached. At the front, this is made from various pieces of printed fabric (floral and brown striped). At the sides, the fabric is gusseted (to allow for the volume of the tubular element at the lower half of the wooden board), and the excess fabric from the gussets is basted close along the edge of the wood, with the excess fabric ends left to dangle/act as streamers. The base fabric is not visible at the back face, as these decorations are sewn down and do not move in the same way the front lappets do. Foundation Layers (Body):2 layers of fabricinnermost layer: are coarse, undyed + indigo dyed(?) linen/hemp (?) fabricsouter layer: printed/dyed cotton fabricsGeneral shape is a large tube, which has been sewn around the bottom circumference of the base fabric covering the wooden armature at the top edgeFront face is flat, while the back face is pleated; there is gusseting at both sides to give more volumeIn general, the two layers of fabric are seamed together along the larger seams (i.e. they do not move completely independently and are more cohesive)In many areas, the general shapes (especially the gussets) have been patched together from a variety of smaller pieces of fabric There is a strip of fabric at the CF interior, near an open seam at the base of the netting, whose purpose is unknownSewn into one of the seams in the large gusset at the back PR side there is a single glove Front:Top element: bundled length of fabric, tied to top edge with repeating sections of doubled dark brown cotton thread, generally knotted at the top. The exterior fabric is striped in design and has a pile, the lining is striped with no pile, and the entire element is edged with green triangular felt. This element extends further than the top edge, with the ends dangling to either side of the top edge. Each side is further decorated with 3 small lappets; each lappet is edged with yellow triangular felt and has a single punched metal element on the front face.Top edge: overlapping small lappets (3-5 layers deep), with a somewhat haphazard attachment pattern - most sewn to base fabric, some sewn to other lappets; attached in a variety of angles. Sides of top edge: there are 4 small lappets on either side that are attached perpendicular to the ones along the top edge (e.g. they are attached along the side of the wooden board) - these also dangle at an angle when the costume is upright. These side lappets are similar in shape and construction to the ones along the top edge. Center front (netting): in the top half of the body, in the area below the internal armature, there is a long rectangular area of netting (technique determination needed). This is flanked by 2 decorative lappets whose sides are sewn down to prevent movement (distinct from the other lappets that are all only attached along their top edges). This netting would allow the wearer of the costume some degree of visibility. The netting is knotted in a diamond pattern, with alternating colors of blue and undyed yarns. Center front (cross bar): at the base of the netting is a smaller tubular element that appears to be similar to that found attached to the wooden board (roll of fabric wrapped with caning and covered in fabric); covering this cross bar is a double-sided lappet whose ends dangle free, containing three smaller lappets on either end (similar to the rolled fabric element attached along the top edge). Attached to the bottom edge of the cross bar is a row of small lappets, which sit atop a variety of longer lappets that extend to the bottom edge. The bottommost lappets attached to the crossbar are quite wide, extending almost its entire width. Sides: flanking the central area to either side is a series of overlapping lappets of varying lengths. Most extend all the way to the bottom edge of the costume, but a few extend ⅔ or ½ of the way down; these smaller lappets are often more highly decorated. Back:Top edge: the back top edge is flat (the face of the board opposite the tubular element, so it does not slope the same way the front edge does) and covered with fabric. There is a row of lappets that are spaced out along the length, interspersed with round mirrors, whose bottom edges are sewn down to prevent movement. Along the bottom edge of the wooden board is a series of small triangular lappets with yarn fringe tassels at their bottom pointsThe entire back face of the Egungun is covered in overlapping lappets. There are various long, overlapping layers of full-length lappets that extend to the bottom edge, covered by a series of mid-length lappets, which are covered in turn by a series of short lappets, which run along the bottom of the wooden armature element Lappets (general): Lappet construction follows the same general pattern:Exterior face is patchwork and constructed with repeating designsLining/reverse tends to be single fabrics, or multiple fabrics that are not decoratively pieced. Edges are generally finished with binding Edges are generally embellished with triangular decoration (like miniature bunting); generally but not always made of felt. (Also cut from fabric, plastic, and yarn fringe)Some exterior lappet faces are further embellished with buttons, mirrors, small punched metal elements, coins, and small fabric-wrapped squares. Many of the lappets are attached directly to the lappet below (instead of to the ground fabric layers)Some lappets have extended lengths, due to the attachment of additional lappetsSome lappets are further decorated with one or more yarn tasselsMost lappets are roughly rectangular in shape, though there are a series of small triangular lappets found on both the front and back
web_text: Egúngún is an ongoing Yoruba masking tradition, encompassing many different types of masquerades that are created and performed to honor ancestors and family lines at various ceremonies and celebrations. An egúngún ensemble is the medium through which ancestors are channeled into the world of the living. One of many different types of egúngún with varied ceremonial roles, paka egúngún are characterized by a wooden horizontal bar across the top of the costume, from which the lappets of the costume are suspended, which sits on the masker's head and forms the rectangular shape of the costume. Aside from the beauty of the costume, its lappets are layered with meaning. The many layers, built up over time, the hundreds of fabrics joined together make this egúngún a living archive. Egúngún is both rooted in a specific place—this particular style is specific to Yoruba culture hailing from Oyo state—and also global in nature, with varied textiles providing a snapshot of the trade of textiles and popular tastes in Nigeria within a global market during the time it was made. Egúngún masquerades, both the garments themselves and their activation, are spiritually significant across African diasporic cultures that continue practice traditional Yoruba religion.
didactic_label: Cloth plays in am important role in the world of the Yoruba, whose myths equate nakedness with infancy, insanity, or the lack of social responsibility. Elaborate dress reflects social power and prestige and , in the Egungun ceremony, is the major medium through which the masker's transformation is achieved.  The Egungun costume, with its multiple layers of prized and costly fabrics, expresses the wealth and status of a family as well as the power of its ancestors.
